name: Trait ascription bias
statement: People hand fixed personality traits to others and call their own behaviour situation-dependent, a gap a preregistered replication with 878 people put at Cohen's f = 0.10.
meaning: The claim is about description, not explanation. Given a pair of opposing adjectives and a third option reading "depends on the situation", people are said to pick a trait more often for someone else and the situational option more often for themselves. The measure is a forced choice repeated over many adjective pairs, and the score is the count of trait choices. A second version of the claim uses consistency ratings: people rate their own trait-related behaviour as varying more from occasion to occasion than another person's. A third version asks how much predictive weight personality carries for self against other. The claim is distinct from the actor-observer asymmetry, which is about the causes people cite when they explain a behaviour, and from the fundamental attribution error, which is about inferring a trait from behaviour a situation forced. This site carries entries on both, and the three are routinely merged.

origin.who: Richard E. Nisbett, Craig Caputo, Patricia Legant and Jeanne Marecek
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: The trait questionnaire was run earlier by Nisbett and Caputo and circulated as an unpublished 1971 Yale manuscript titled "Personality Traits: Why Other People Do the Things They Do". Jones and Nisbett describe it in their monograph under the heading "Personality Traits Are Things Other People Have", and it reached print as one of the studies in the 1973 paper.

evidence: Jones and Nisbett report the design in full. Twenty polar adjective dimensions, such as reserved against emotionally expressive and lenient against firm, each came with a third option reading "depends on the situation". Male college students checked one of the three for each pair for five people: themselves, their best friend, an age peer they liked but did not know well, their father, and the television commentator Walter Cronkite. Subjects took the situational option for themselves and assigned traits readily to the other four. Neither acquaintance nor similarity in age moved the result much, and traits went to the four others in about equal numbers. Kammer separated intensity from variability in 1982 and found that 56 people judged their friends' behaviour more consistent than their own while giving themselves the higher trait intensities. Baxter and Goldberg had subjects rate themselves and a same-sex peer they knew well on 60 adjectives, from -3 to +3 with four middle options including "depends on the situation", and then rate the consistency of the behaviour behind each judgement. For 72% of the 60 traits the majority of subjects described themselves as more variable than the other person. Pronin and Kugler asked 58 Princeton undergraduates to draw box models predicting behaviour, sizing a box for each of four predictors. Own personality took 21% of the predictive weight against 32% for a roommate's, F(1, 54) = 24.42, p < 0.0001, while own desires and intentions took 36% against 27%.

replication.headline: The self-other gap in trait ascription turned up again in 878 people at Cohen's f = 0.10 against the original 0.35, while the trait asymmetry measured through behaviour explanations pools at d = 0.09 and misses significance.
replication.detail: Adelina and Feldman ran a preregistered replication of Pronin and Ross's Studies 1 to 3, recruiting 911 American MTurk workers and keeping 878 after preregistered exclusions. Their instrument merged the two original scales into 22 items, each offering two opposing traits and a third option reading "variable/depends on the situation", with target assigned between subjects. Participants ascribed 17.02 traits on average when judging a friend and 16.16 when judging themselves, F(1, 876) = 9.02, p = 0.003, Cohen's f = 0.10. The original effect was f = 0.35, 95% confidence interval 0.09 to 0.61. They class the outcome as signal inconsistent and smaller. The paper prints three different intervals for its own f: 0.03 to 0.16 in the abstract, 0.04 to 0.17 in the results text and in Table 5, and 0.05 to 0.16 in a footnote. Cohen's f is not a metric this site's structured effect-size fields accept, so those figures stay in prose. Against that, Malle, Knobe and Nelson tested a trait version of the actor-observer hypothesis across nine studies, over 1,300 participants and 8,000 explanations, and found the trait asymmetry at a precision-weighted d of 0.09, not significant. Malle's earlier meta-analysis reaches the same place from the other side: among the 61 studies in his pool where traits dominated the internal attributions, the asymmetry was d = 0.098, 95% confidence interval -0.011 to 0.207.

study.cite: Adelina, N., & Feldman, G. (2021). Are past and future selves perceived differently from present self? Replication and extension of Pronin and Ross (2006) temporal differences in trait self-ascription. International Review of Social Psychology, 34(1), 29.

limits: The versions of the claim do not travel together. Kammer's subjects gave themselves the less consistent behaviour and the stronger traits at the same time, which is awkward for any account in which the self is simply seen as trait-free. White argued that the rate at which people pick a trait rather than a situation is set by the response format: across formats varying the number of trait and situation options, trait responding stayed close to chance expectancy, and he concluded that no inference about natural trait-ascription frequency can be drawn from those absolute rates. He added that this leaves self-other differences untouched. Design matters too. Adelina and Feldman assigned the target between subjects, as Pronin and Ross had. On the neighbouring claim that people see their own lives as less predictable than a peer's, Chandrashekar and colleagues ran three preregistered replications of Pronin and Kugler's Experiment 1 and found d = -0.33, 95% confidence interval -0.52 to -0.14, with 424 people judging self or other, and d = 0.00, 95% confidence interval -0.10 to 0.10, with 434 people judging both. Their reading is that people correct the asymmetry once the two judgements sit side by side. Baxter and Goldberg's subjects did describe both persons, so the pattern is not confined to single-target designs, but no preregistered within-subject test of the trait-versus-situation forced choice was located. Searches of Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, PubMed and Europe PMC found no test of that forced choice outside Western samples. The founding study used male college students only.
misreadings: The bias is not the actor-observer asymmetry, and the two entries on this site reach different verdicts because they measure different things. Malle's meta-analysis of 173 studies of causal explanations gives d = 0.095, and Malle, Knobe and Nelson's trait figure of 0.09 belongs to that same explanation-coding tradition. What Adelina and Feldman replicated was a forced choice between adjectives, which asks people to describe rather than to explain. Nor is it the fundamental attribution error, which concerns a trait inferred from behaviour the situation compelled. The claim is also weaker than the slogan suggests. Adelina and Feldman's two means, 17.02 for a friend and 16.16 for the self out of 22 items, sit close together, so people were not declining to describe themselves in traits. Raw percentages of trait responses are the figure most often quoted from this literature and the one White's analysis says carries no information about people, only about the answer sheet. The name is not the literature's. Papers say trait ascription or self-other asymmetry; a Crossref bibliographic search for the exact phrase "trait ascription bias" returned one title, Parvini's 2015 chapter on Iago and Othello.
